newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic may use carrot and stick tactic in Serbia.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic may use carrot and stick tactic in Serbia.

text.p: President Slobodan Milosevic may try to deal with Serbia's wave of street protests with a mixture of repression and concession, political analysts believe.
He may crack down on the demonstrators but at the same time sack unpopular ministers who are widely blamed for economic hardships.
Either way, the moment of truth is fast approaching in the marathon battle of wills, the analysts believe.

After 51 straight days of street protests against election fraud, neo-communist hardliners and moderates in Milosevic's coterie are still debating whether to crack down, compromise or concede but feel the reclusive president must act now.

Milosevic has been humiliated by the tenacity and witty ingenuity of the protesters but has tolerated them so far in part to avoid derailing Belgrade's campaign for re-admission to international institutions after four years of U.N. sanctions.
His hand will soon be forced by events however.

The independent daily Nasa Borba said Milosevic was preparing to ban protest gatherings shortly not only in the streets -- a measure imposed after a December 24 riot involving pro-Socialist party (SPS) thugs -- but also in pedestrian zones.
It said he hopes this would stop a rot of repressive vigour in his vaunted paramilitary police caused by the government's prolonged indecision and blandishments from protesters.

"Milosevic is nervous that after almost two months of protests, even the police on whose loyalty he counts are losing morale and discipline as a result of...successful attempts by demonstrators to "soften them up,'" Nasa Borba said.

Members of the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition have begun a charm offensive against police. They marked Orthodox Christmas Day on Tuesday by walking along a cordon of police kissing them on the cheeks or their riot helmet visors.
Milosevic cannot afford to lose the loyalty of his police because the army, disgruntled at SPS neglect, supports Zajedno's goals and has vowed not to crush protests as it did in 1991 on his orders.

Political sources say Milosevic may also shuffle his cabinet to placate discontent over a shambolic economy without accepting Zajedno's main demand -- the re-instatement of opposition victories in municipal elections annulled by the SPS.

Analysts expect Milosevic to sack Prime Minister Mirko Marjanovic, blamed for allowing pre-election price increases victimising the poor and not releasing money to pay overdue pensions -- mistakes that boosted Zajedno.
"There is a struggle between different (SPS) factions eager to get close to and influence Milosevic and remove his obviously incompetent associates," Nasa Borba said.
"This could pave the way for some sort of compromise with the opposition, who have surprised (everyone) with their endurance and imagination."

Analysts say only mass strikes by workers in support of Zajedno could bring the government swiftly to its knees. But walkouts have not transpired as many workers are struggling to make ends meet and remain wedded to socialist rule.
Fearing a police swoop, Zajedno has added civil disobedience to its political armoury.
It has called for supporters to swamp the switchboards of government offices with nuisance calls. Another possible gambit is non-payment of utility bills and state television fees.
"All this can't go on forever," one Western envoy said.

"The hardliners may ultimately prevail with a crackdown, arguing that Serbia has been offered only sticks rather than carrots from the West and has little to gain no matter what happens," he told Reuters.

"Milosevic might look around and notice that Russia was not sanctioned by the West for its bloody intervention in Chechnya, that Croatia and Albania got away with election shenanigans but weren't sanctioned either," he said.
